To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mass of a cluster is proportional to the square of its richness and to the fourth power of its luminosity, with a scatter in each case of {approx}13%.
the mean mass of a cluster of galaxies is proportional to the square root of the optical luminosity of the cluster's brightest member, and to the square of the number of galaxies in the cluster.

the mean 3-D mass profile of galaxy clusters in SDSS can be inferred from the measured 2-D shear profile, and that the mean mass of a cluster is well correlated with the cluster optical luminosity and the cluster richness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the statistical properties of galaxy clusters in the optical and X-ray, the connection between these two observables and the cluster dark matter halos.
the measurement of the X-ray luminosity-optical richness relation for a large sample of galaxy clusters.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mean mass-richness relation is well constrained, but the scatter of that relation is poorly constrained.
the X-ray luminosity-optical richness relation for galaxy clusters is not linear, and that the scatter is larger than expected.
the X-ray luminosity-optical richness relation for maxBCG galaxy clusters is well understood and can be used as a robust proxy for mass.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optical richness and luminosities are good proxies for the cluster mass, and that the scatter in this relation is not large, {approx} 30% in the mass range of 10^13.5-10^15 M_sun.
we have shown that we can measure the mean mass and mass distribution of a cluster from weak lensing data alone, and we have shown that these measurements agree with the predictions of LCDM models.
the cluster-mass relation is tight and well understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we are able to constrain the mean halo mass and concentration of the maxBCG clusters with a precision that is comparable to that of the most precise cluster mass measurements in the literature.
the mean X-ray luminosity-optical richness relation can be used to predict the mean X-ray properties of clusters with a precision of about 20%.
the optical richness is a very robust proxy for cluster mass.
